intro: Awadagin Pratt plays the Étude in D♯ minor, Op. 8 No. 12, Patetico, a piano piece about two minutes long. The melody is in octaves over a left hand that leaps across the keyboard, and in the return the material is shared between both hands.

sections.label: A · Octaves above a leaping bass
sections.mNote: Right-hand melody in octaves; the left hand leaps across the keyboard.

sections.label: B · Octave melody over left-hand triplets
sections.mNote: The melody continues in octaves over continuing left-hand triplets.

sections.label: A′ · Melody over two-hand triplet chords
sections.mNote: Both hands now play triplet chords beneath the tune.

sections.label: Coda · Climb and three chords
sections.mNote: Both hands climb before the final D♯ minor chords.

relations.label: The octave melody returns
relations.basis: The A′ section intensifies the opening D♯-minor material after the quieter middle. These excerpts compare a phrase from the first section with its return inside the section marked near 64 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.930, sustained 12 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 51 s (cache/form/scriabin-etude-op8-12.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Right-hand octaves, bars 1–16
cues.text: Scriabin marks the étude Patetico. The right hand plays the melody in octaves while the left hand leaps between bass notes and widely spaced chords. The melody moves in twos against the accompaniment’s threes.
cues.evidence: Scriabin, Op. 8 No. 12, bars 1–16; score typeset by Scott Gorrie (2007), pp. 2–3. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f3/IMSLP273680-PMLP07375-Scriabin_Op.8_No_12.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Belyayev, March 1895
cues.text: In March 1895 Scriabin was still revising the études, and his publisher, Belyayev, was waiting for them. Scriabin wrote that he worked from the time he got up until evening: “I do not want to publish anything unfinished.” The D♯ minor étude was among the pieces he had rewritten.
cues.evidence: Scriabin to Mitrofan Belyayev, March 1895, Letters, edited by Alexey Kashperov (2003), pp. 91–92; quoted in Valentina Rubcova’s preface to Henle HN 1486. Translation from the German quotation. https://www.henle.de/media/56/3c/dd/1697725817/1486-1697725817-sync.pdf

cues.title: Return of the opening theme
cues.text: The opening theme returns in D♯ minor, with triplet chords now in both hands. The right hand plays the accompaniment and holds the longer melody above it. Both hands then climb towards the final chords.
cues.evidence: Scriabin, Op. 8 No. 12, bars 34–55; Scott Gorrie typesetting (2007), pp. 4–6. The return begins at A tempo; bars 52–55 contain the ascent and closing chords. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f3/IMSLP273680-PMLP07375-Scriabin_Op.8_No_12.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: White House workshop, 2009
cues.text: On 4 November 2009 Awadagin Pratt played this étude at a classical-music workshop and concert at the White House. Michelle Obama introduced Pratt, Joshua Bell, Alisa Weilerstein and Sharon Isbin as “the best in the world”. She added that Pratt had begun on a dusty upright his mother bought for a hundred dollars.
cues.evidence: Remarks by the First Lady at the Classical Music Series workshops, East Room, 2:22 p.m., 4 November 2009 (“They are the best in the world, and we’re incredibly lucky to have them today”; Pratt’s dusty upright piano “for just a hundred dollars”), with the video of the one-hour workshop and concert, White House page “White House Workshop: Classical Music” (the transcript carries the release date 26 October 2009). https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/photos-and-video/video/white-house-workshop-classical-music The Commons description of this recording places Pratt’s performance of the étude at about 29:40–31:44 of that video. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:20091104_Awadagin_Pratt_-_Scriabin,_%C3%89tude_Op._8_No._12.ogg

transitions.title: Diminuendo to piano over continuing triplets
transitions.from: A · Octaves above a leaping bass
transitions.to: B · Octave melody over left-hand triplets
transitions.how: Scriabin writes diminuendo, then piano, and the octave melody moves into a more winding phrase. The left hand continues its triplets and wide leaps through the change.
transitions.evidence: Scriabin, Op. 8 No. 12, bars 16–19; Scott Gorrie typesetting (2007), p. 3. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f3/IMSLP273680-PMLP07375-Scriabin_Op.8_No_12.pdf

transitions.title: Triplet chords in both hands
transitions.from: B · Octave melody over left-hand triplets
transitions.to: A′ · Melody over two-hand triplet chords
transitions.how: A crescendo and a brief ritardando lead to the return. At A tempo the D♯ minor melody comes back above low bass octaves, and the accompaniment is now spread across both hands. The right hand holds the tune and repeats chords beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Scriabin, Op. 8 No. 12, bars 32–36; Scott Gorrie typesetting (2007), p. 4. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f3/IMSLP273680-PMLP07375-Scriabin_Op.8_No_12.pdf

transitions.title: Up the keyboard, then three chords
transitions.from: A′ · Melody over two-hand triplet chords
transitions.how: The two hands climb the keyboard together. A rest cuts short their last high chord. Two more chords follow lower down, and the second of these is held for a whole bar. All three chords are D♯ minor.
transitions.evidence: Scriabin, Op. 8 No. 12, bars 52–55; Scott Gorrie typesetting (2007), p. 6. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f3/IMSLP273680-PMLP07375-Scriabin_Op.8_No_12.pdf

composer.epithet: Composer who wrote a part for coloured light that had to be omitted at the work’s first performance.
facts: Moscow Conservatory, 1888–92: Safonov, Taneyev and Arensky
Piano professor at the Moscow Conservatory from 1898
Publisher Mitrofan Belyayev; conductor Serge Koussevitzky
Ten piano sonatas; three symphonies; a concerto; The Poem of Ecstasy and Prometheus
composer.background:
At the Moscow première of Prometheus in 1911, Scriabin sat at the piano and Serge Koussevitzky conducted. The audience heard the large orchestra, the solo piano and the sustained harmonies that precede the first horn melody. One part of the score was not performed: the keyboard intended to project coloured light. Alexander Mozer had built a small apparatus for Scriabin, but because of technical difficulties Scriabin withdrew it from the concert, and the première went ahead without the lights.

He was born in Moscow in 1872. His mother, Lyubov, was a trained pianist; she died when he was a baby. His father was pursuing a diplomatic career abroad, and his aunt, also Lyubov, helped bring him up. He entered the cadet corps in 1882, took lessons from Nikolai Zverev, and joined Vasily Safonov’s piano class at the Moscow Conservatory in 1888. Rachmaninoff studied there too. Scriabin graduated as a pianist in 1892, a year after Rachmaninoff, but left without completing the composition course with Sergei Taneyev and Anton Arensky.
